30 Days of Vibe Coding | Day 23: Tests as Your Safety Net — Unit Testing with Vitest
Ever heard that one? From a security point of view, a lot of security holes come down to human error.
People forget, cut corners, and act on a whim. No matter how careful you are, something will still slip through.
So in this post we're going to look at a concept built on "people can't be trusted": testing.
For a lot of beginners, testing is probably a pretty unfamiliar word.
But you've actually already been doing it. It's the "review" step I keep going on about.

Every time you asked the AI to change a feature or add a new one, I had you run through the review again and again to make sure nothing broke — things like adding an expense, checking whether it shows up in the list, refreshing to see if the data is still there, and so on.
So what we're going to do now is turn that "testing process" into something automated — a program that does all of this for us.
Not sure why that's a big deal? In short, review work that used to take you hours becomes something that runs on its own at the push of a button.

On top of that, it becomes what's called a "safety net." Whenever you change the code, this safety net checks whether anything got broken, so you don't end up changing feature A, breaking feature B, and never finding out.
Huh? You have to be picky about what you test?
Yep. Not every feature needs tests. Picking the feature that would hurt "the most" if it broke and testing that is the most efficient way to go.
So which features count as the ones that hurt "the most"? For our money-note, it's anything to do with calculating money.
Which ones are those? For example...

So why use this as the thing we learn on? Simple: pure functions aren't tied to the UI or to storage, so they're the easiest to test. And when the logic is solid before it gets wired to the screen, it's easier to review too, because the result is either right or wrong — no gray area. Testing through the UI is a whole different story.

If you try this yourself and end up with a different number of tests or different test cases, that's totally normal. AI has some randomness built in, so the number of cases won't be the same every time. We're just doing our best to constrain its behavior with SPEC.md and the prompt, so the cases it generates stay within the boundaries we asked for.
Even though the AI writes the test cases, you still need to roughly understand what they're testing and what they say. Otherwise, how would you know the tests it wrote are right?
The good news is that test cases are a lot easier to read than regular code, because most of them are just "put this in, expect that out." You only need to understand what's being tested.

Still confusing? No worries, I'll go through it line by line:
Groups the test cases inside it together. You usually put the name of the function being tested here, so you know what this group is testing.
This is a single test case, with a description of the case inside. The description is usually the expected result (this one reads "0 shows as $0").
This is the core of the whole test.
means "I expect," and inside the parentheses goes the actual result.
means "the result has to be exactly this." So the whole line in plain English is: I expect

So a test case is just a description of "put this in, expect that out." You've probably noticed tests are a lot easier to read than code, because they describe "how this function behaves." Whether that behavior matches what we expect is exactly what testing is for.

In software engineering, there's an approach called "Test-Driven Development (TDD)," where you write the test cases first, then write the code, and finally run the tests to see if they pass.
This way you think through how the function should behave before you write any code, which helps you avoid writing code that doesn't do what you expected.
Controlled failure exercise: make it fail once

Next, we're going to make a mistake on purpose. Yep, you read that right — on purpose. Otherwise, how would you know the tests actually work? And having a failing case is what shows you what tests are really worth.
First, give the AI this prompt:
Please deliberately break formatAmount so the "thousands separator" case is missing the $ in front, then run the tests once and show me the results.
If all goes as expected, you should see the AI tell you the tests failed.

With tests as your safety net, whenever you add or change a feature, the tests will fail if you didn't update the test cases to match, or if you broke the existing code. Then you know what you broke, and it's a lot easier to track down the problem.
But once you've seen it fail, remember to change it back, or your project really will stay broken. The easiest way is to just tell the AI:
Please restore the formatAmount you just broke on purpose, then run the tests again to confirm everything passes.

No matter which step you're at or how far along the build is, there's one thing you'll keep doing over and over:
. But you don't have to remember it yourself or keep telling the AI — especially since the AI might forget about it once the Context gets too long.
So we can use a Hook to run the tests automatically. That way, every time the AI finishes something, it's guaranteed to run the tests for you, and you never have to worry about forgetting.
I'm not going to walk through how to do it here, though. Give it a try yourself!
We're about at the end, so here's a quick summary:
Testing turns the manual review you've been doing all along into an automated program.
You don't need to test everything. Start with the part where a mistake would hurt the most.
You don't need to understand the code to direct the AI to write tests. Your prompt just needs to clearly describe the situations you care about.
Test cases are a lot easier to read than code — it's just "put this in, expect that out."
One last reminder, though: passing tests doesn't mean the feature has no problems. A lot of the UI/UX on screen still needs you to review it yourself.
